clue.text: Hull supporters may be put up here

definitions.text: Hull supporters may be put up here

parts.words: Hull supporters may be put up here
parts.note: reads like lodging for fans of the Yorkshire football club, but means a place where the frames holding a vessel's hull are erected

explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire with a football club, so 'Hull supporters' and 'put up' (given a bed) suggest fans' lodgings; here the hull is a ship's body and 'put up' means built.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipbuilder's yard is where keels, frames and hulls are constructed.

clue.text: What's left of the Rhone wine Monsieur put out?

indicators.note: put out means the abbreviation is ejected from the wine name

parts.note: Hermitage is a celebrated wine from the northern Rhone

explanation.surface: A Frenchman pours away his Rhone wine and someone asks what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A heritage is what is handed down and remains from the past.

clue.text: Moving, one can pitch any quantity into it

definitions.text: Moving, one can pitch any quantity into it

indicators.note: moving says the letters of the three words are shifted into another order

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number in maths

explanation.surface: Moving house, you can throw any amount into the big van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' scrambles ONECANPITCH; N follows. The whole clue also describes a removal van, which you load with any amount when moving house.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantechnicon is a large furniture-removal van, filled with belongings on moving day.

clue.text: Moving artist to make the soul rise?

parts.note: anima is Latin for the soul, used in Jungian psychology
a tor is a rocky hill, a rise in the ground

explanation.surface: An inspiring artist whose work makes the spirit soar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' sounds like emotionally stirring; it means making pictures move, as in cartoons.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartoon-film maker draws images that appear to move.

clue.text: Deputy Lieutenant accepts more of the Right

indicators.note: accepts means the abbreviation takes the other word inside it

parts.note: DL is the abbreviation for Deputy Lieutenant, a county official
extra means more or additional

explanation.surface: A county official welcomes more right-wingers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Right' suggests politics; it is simply the right-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: Dextral means right-handed or on the right side, from Latin dexter.

clue.text: Adviser of women in medley-relay

indicators.note: in places the women abbreviation inside the jumbled word
a medley is a mixture, so the letters of relay are mixed

explanation.surface: A coach advising the women's team in a swimming medley relay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medley' scrambles RELAY to LAYER, and 'in' puts W inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A solicitor or barrister gives legal counsel to clients.

clue.text: Coin once clutched by Indian nanny?

indicators.note: clutched by means the letters are held within the words that follow

explanation.surface: An old coin held tight by an Indian children's nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: The anna was a former Indian coin, a sixteenth of a rupee.
explanation.definitionFit: The anna was a former coin of British India worth a sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Short fat Bill, we hear, could be a : cardinal

indicators.note: short means the fat word is cut by its final letter

parts.note: gross means fat or obese
a bird's bill is its beak

explanation.surface: A stout fellow called Bill, rumour says, might become a prince of the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' poses as a man's name and 'cardinal' as a churchman; both are birds' terms. 'we hear' points to the sound of 'gross beak'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cardinal is a North American finch of the thick-billed group so named.

clue.text: Setter for whom one sits?

parts.note: a setter here is the person who sets a test paper, and candidates sit that paper for them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' suggests a crossword setter or a dog posing for its owner; it is the person who sets an exam that candidates sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The official who writes and marks a test is the one candidates sit papers for.

clue.text: Some herring — first of catch — escaped

indicators.note: first of tells us to take only the opening letter of the word catch

parts.note: escaped means ran away, so ran

explanation.surface: A fishing report: some of the herring catch got away.
explanation.walkthrough: A cran is an old Scottish measure of fresh herring, about 750 fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A cran is a unit for measuring a quantity of landed herring.

clue.text: Fodder ass might try? Nothing to mix!

indicators.note: to mix says the letters of the preceding words and the nought are to be stirred together into a new order

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A donkey might sample some feed, needing nothing mixed into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to mix' scrambles ASSMIGHTTRY together with O (from 'Nothing'): the clue explicitly adds the O into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Timothy is a meadow grass grown as hay for livestock feed.

clue.text: Once a third-class seat could be acquired here

definitions.text: Once a third-class seat could be acquired here

parts.words: Once a third-class seat could be acquired here
parts.note: sounds like buying a cheap train ticket; a riding was once a third of Yorkshire, and a seat is a rider's position on a horse

explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire was historically split into three Ridings; a good 'seat' is how a rider sits a horse, learned at such a school.
explanation.definitionFit: An equestrian academy is where pupils learn to sit a horse well.

clue.text: Mother fine, the lucky thing!

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
scot is an old word for a payment, tax or fine, as in scot-free

explanation.surface: Good news: mother is fine, what a lucky thing!
explanation.walkthrough: SCOT survives in 'scot-free', meaning without paying the levy.
explanation.definitionFit: A team's charm is something carried or displayed to bring good luck.

clue.text: Dog taken out to drink?

parts.note: something taken out into the open is aired, as clothes or a dog given an outing
ale is a beer, something to drink

explanation.surface: A dog taken out for walkies, or for a pint?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a dog walk ending at the pub; the pieces are simply AIRED and ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Airedale is a large terrier breed from Yorkshire.

clue.text: A residence, not necessarily rural

parts.note: a church official's house, alluding to the rural dean, though cathedral clergy of that title live in towns

explanation.walkthrough: A rural dean is a Church of England priest over a group of parishes; the clergy house named after the office also belongs to cathedral deans in cities.
explanation.definitionFit: The official house of a dean in the church is named after that office.

clue.text: Collapse of blue flag?

parts.note: feeling blue means feeling down
to flag is to droop or fall

explanation.surface: A blue flag slips down the pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruin or fall from power is a collapse.

clue.text: Pair stuck in fissure get the wind up in the Rockies

indicators.note: stuck in means the pair is pushed inside the crack word

parts.note: a chink is a narrow crack or fissure
a pair in cricket is two ducks, scores of nought, so two O letters

explanation.surface: Someone takes fright in the Rocky Mountains after two things get wedged in a crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get the wind up' (be scared) is a red herring: the definition is a wind up in the Rockies. A pair in cricket is out for nought in both innings.
explanation.definitionFit: The chinook is a warm dry wind blowing down the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains.

clue.text: Good place for Norman Archer as things turned out

indicators.note: turned out signals the letters are rearranged into a new result

explanation.surface: Things worked out well for a Norman bowman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norman archers won the battle of 1066 at this East Sussex town.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1066 battle there was won by William the Conqueror's bowmen.

clue.text: Blanket stitch originally used for dungarees

parts.note: blanket as an adjective means total or overall

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of the word stitch

explanation.surface: Blanket stitch was used to edge some work trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blanket stitch' is a real embroidery stitch, a trap: 'Blanket' is the adjective meaning covering everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Overalls are protective trousers with a bib, much like dungarees.

clue.text: Silver bullet stuck

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a round is a single bullet or shell

explanation.surface: A silver bullet is lodged in something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver bullet' reads as a magic remedy; it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship stuck on the bottom in shallow water is said to have run onto ground.

clue.text: Custodian Mark, a mean fellow!

parts.note: to mark is to heed or observe, to watch
a dog is slang for a contemptible, mean man

explanation.surface: A guard named Mark is denounced as a nasty piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' poses as a man's name; it is the verb meaning to observe.
explanation.definitionFit: A guardian body or person keeping watch over others' conduct is a custodian of standards.

clue.text: Pain had upset one in bed…

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns both words upside down so they read backwards

parts.note: to ail is to pain or trouble

explanation.surface: Someone poorly takes to their bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one in bed' suggests an invalid; it is a plant in a flower bed. 'upset' reverses AIL HAD into DAH LIA.
explanation.definitionFit: This tuberous flowering plant is grown in garden borders.

clue.text: Theory and practice?

explanation.definitionFit: A system can be an organised theory, such as a philosophical scheme, or a method of working, such as a betting routine.

clue.text: Finish like the Paris-Warsaw alliance

explanation.definitionFit: A glossy shellac coating for wood is a type of furniture finish; a pact between Paris and Warsaw would be a Franco-Polish one.

clue.text: work-unit needs oxygen, therefore

parts.note: the erg is a unit of work in the CGS system
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: The patient in bed needs oxygen, so the work must stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to the previous clue's sickbed scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for so or hence.

clue.text: Just out of Lyon

indicators.note: out of here suggests the letters of the French city name are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: A traveller has only just left Lyon.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and merely both mean nothing more than.

clue.text: This mission has a member at No. 10 before noon

indicators.note: before places the preceding pieces ahead of the letter for noon

parts.note: a leg is a limb, one of the body's members
taken as written
10 written as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: A diplomatic visit includes someone calling at Downing Street before noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No. 10' suggests Downing Street, the British prime minister's address; here the figures 1 and 0 become I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A legation is a diplomatic mission headed by a minister, lower than an embassy.

clue.text: Show record drop

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record
to drop a game or point is to lose it

explanation.surface: A music show or record sales take a dip.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something is to show it.
